items.label: Years building systems that have to stay up

pains.title: Six things that break, and what replaces them
pains.intro: Every one of these came out of running a real shop. If none of them sound familiar, you probably don't need this.

stock.moment: The counter sold the last one at 11:40. The website sold it again at 13:10. Now you are phoning a customer to take the order back.
stock.promise: One stock number, shared by the till, the warehouse and the website.
stock.proof: Counter sales draw down web stock instantly, and the count is checked again at the moment of purchase.

money.moment: Card sales in the bank app, the marketplace settlement in an email, supplier invoices in a folder, cost of goods in your head. So you price by feel and never find out which products lose money.
money.promise: Ask in plain language, get the figure with cost of goods already in it.
money.proof: Weighted average cost kept per item, profit and loss against real costs, and sales history for every product.

commission.misery: A good month costs me more.
commission.moment: Subscription, commission on every order, three apps to patch the gaps. All in a currency you don't earn in, all rising with your success.
commission.promise: One build fee. Ten times the orders costs the same as one.
commission.proof: No per-sale commission, no per-seat licence, running on your own hosting and your own database.

catalog.misery: The box is still by the door.
catalog.moment: Stock arrived on the 3rd. Photos, descriptions, technical specifications, then all of it again in two more languages. It is the 14th. You have paid for goods nobody can buy yet.
catalog.promise: Paste the supplier sheet and get filterable products in every language, unpublished until you have looked.
catalog.proof: Spec sheets parsed into product attributes, machine translation filling the rest, every line editable by hand.

orders.misery: The address came as a voice message.
orders.moment: A screenshot of the item, is it available, the price agreed in one thread and the address in another. Nothing countable, and the shop cannot run without you inside it.
orders.promise: Web, counter, marketplace and phone orders in one queue, each with its own status.
orders.proof: A single queue across channels, manual entry for phone customers, and a Telegram message the moment an order lands.

staff.moment: Your cashier could serve the queue, but the only login you have also shows margins and can delete an order. So the login stays with you, and so does the work.
staff.promise: The cashier sees the till. You see the margins. Both are on the record.
staff.proof: Separate owner, manager and cashier roles, with an audit log of who changed what and when.

also: Changing a delivery fee or an opening time means emailing a developer and waiting
Half the catalog exists in one language, so half your customers see a shop that isn't for them
Marketplace orders arrive in their own queue with their own stock, reconciled by hand on Sunday
Your catalog lives inside Instagram, where Google cannot read it
A single refund is the same arithmetic done three times in three places
The export button gives you a file that imports nowhere
pains.ctaNote: Recognise two or more of these? Send your catalog and see them fixed in your own shop before you pay anything.

steps: You send whatever you already have: a spreadsheet, a WooCommerce export, or photographs of the shelves
I import it and send you a private URL with your own catalog running inside the platform

ai.title: An AI assistant that actually operates the shop
ai.intro: You can talk to your shop the way you would talk to an assistant who never gets bored. Ask what needs attention this morning. Hand over the supplier invoice. Tell it to process a return. Most “AI for e-commerce” is a chatbot bolted onto the storefront to answer customer questions, and this is the opposite. Your store exposes itself as a set of tools over the Model Context Protocol, so Claude, ChatGPT or any MCP-capable assistant can read and change real data, with your permissions, your audit trail, and your approval on anything destructive.
ai.asksTitle: Things you can just ask for
asks: Which products sold worst last month and still have stock sitting in the warehouse?
Add these 12 items from the supplier invoice, translate the descriptions, and leave them unpublished.
Put 15% off everything in the Filaments category until Sunday.
What did we actually earn in March after cost of goods and delivery?
Find every product with a missing photo, no category, or a price below cost.
Order #6162 is coming back. Refund it and put the stock back in the store.

chat.title: into.ge admin · MCP

turns.text: Anything above max stock that has not sold since spring — put it on 20% off until Sunday and feature it on the homepage.

32 items sit above their maximum level, and 14 of those have not sold since May.
−20% on those 14 until Sunday, and they are now the “Clearance” row on the homepage. The other 18 still move, so I left their price alone.
Take this supplier page — pull the description and the photos and make it a product in my shop, all four languages.
read supplier page · create_product · attach_product_image ×6 · import_product_specs · translate_text ×12

Description and 6 photos pulled in, written as a draft in Georgian, English, Ukrainian and Russian.
The spec table off that page became filterable attributes. Left unpublished with the price blank — that part is yours.
QIDI raised their prices 8%. Update ours, but back up first.

Backup taken, then 29 QIDI products repriced +8%.
Two were already selling below cost, so I left those and listed them for you. One click restores the backup if you change your mind.
Every morning, message me on Telegram whatever dropped below the reorder point overnight.

Wired to your Telegram. Today it would have said: 269 items below the reorder point, 249 of them at zero.
Want it grouped by supplier so it doubles as the purchase order?
If a customer asks their own ChatGPT for PETG, does my shop show up?

It does. Four PETG lines come back, three of them in stock, with prices, photos and links to your product pages.
The public server only ever sees the catalogue — orders, costs and customers stay on the admin side.

audit.title: A real answer, from the real store
audit.intro: Asked of into.ge's live catalog while writing this page. I didn't pick a flattering question either: it found problems in the shop I run, which is rather the point.
audit.question: Audit the catalog. Anything broken, mislinked or unpublishable?
findings: 17 published products tracking stock with no inventory item linked
158 links whose product and stock-item names don't match, e.g. "ABS-Like OdorLite" → "eResine ABS Odor Grey"
0 missing translations, missing images, empty categories, bad prices, duplicate barcodes or duplicate SKUs
0 orphaned translation rows, shared stock items or links to retired items
audit.footnote: Thirteen classes of defect, checked across the whole catalog in one question. Finding the same by eye is a morning's work you'd never actually schedule.

shape.title: We shape it to your trade

launch.title: Launch, then keep going
launch.body: Live on your domain and your hosting, staff trained, AI assistant connected. Then ongoing support at whatever level you want. I keep your installation patched and changing as the business does.

shopify.title: Why not just use Shopify?
shopify.intro: Sometimes you should, and I'll say so on the call. Rented platforms are the right answer for a simple catalog with standard needs. This is worth it when one of these is true:
reasons: Shopify's point of sale and payment options don't cover Georgia, so your counter stays a separate system
Your products don't fit the boxes: variants, technical specs, per-location stock, made-to-order work
You're paying for five apps to patch the gaps, and they still don't talk to each other
Your shop floor and your website need to share one stock number and currently don't
You sell in more than one language and the translation add-on is making a mess of it
Per-sale commission has started costing more than software would
You want an AI assistant with real access to your business, not a support-chat widget
You want your customer list and your data on your own infrastructure, not a platform's

explanatory.title: The longer version
body: Every rented shop platform has an opinion about how you should sell, and you spend your first year working around it. Your products don't fit its fields, your delivery rules aren't one of its options, and the gaps get patched with apps that charge monthly and still don't talk to each other. Meanwhile it takes a percentage of every sale, and takes more the better your month goes.

I build one system fitted the other way round. Your product fields are the ones your trade actually uses, your delivery and payment rules are yours, and the modules you don't need are switched off rather than sitting there confusing your staff. The counter and the website draw down the same stock, orders from every channel land in one queue, and the money side knows what things cost, so you can ask what you actually earned and get an answer.

It runs on your own hosting, against your own database. The catalogue, the orders and the customer list stay exportable and yours. When you need something that does not exist yet, I build it and bill it by the hour, and it becomes a real part of your store rather than a private patch.

I am not a platform. I am one developer who built this for a shop in Tbilisi and still runs it. into.ge sells 3D printers and filament on it today, in three languages, with a bank integration and a point of sale. When it breaks on a Saturday, I get the call. Send me your product list and a few days later you get a private link to your own shop with your own products in it, plus an audit of everything broken in your catalogue — yours to keep whether you buy or not.
